text: Welcome to the capstone. Over these three lessons you'll build one complete, tested, deployable pipeline for a real scoped application, bringing together the first six chapters of this course. The scenario: a university's registrar's office needs a Course Registration application, and they've told you what they need in one sentence.

"We need something real. It has to be tested before it goes live, and it absolutely cannot break during the first week of each semester, when every student is trying to register at once." That sentence hides three problems. A real Dev, Test, Prod pipeline from Chapter 1. Verified automated test coverage on the critical path, Chapter 4's job. And a hard deployment-timing constraint, exactly what Chapter 6 covered. This lesson pulls those three apart into real requirements before any building starts.

Requirement one: instance strategy. Development happens exclusively in Dev. Nothing touches Prod directly, because an undocumented quick fix in Prod creates drift the moment you try to promote the next change. Test is where registrar staff do user acceptance testing safely. Requirement two: Source Control. The application connects to a Git repository from day one, so every change becomes a reviewable pull request instead of an opaque Update Set — the IT director specifically asked for this paper trail after a past vendor's undocumented changes caused problems. Requirement three: ATF coverage on the critical path — a student registering for a course, including what happens when a section is full.

Requirement four is how the pipeline meets Change Management. Chapter 5 drew out the real tension between change velocity and change control, and this capstone resolves it the same way: every promotion from Test to Prod still goes through a real Change Request, with the ATF Test Suite's pass or fail result attached as evidence. The pipeline doesn't replace the Change Advisory Board's judgment — it gives that board something real to approve instead of something to take on faith.

And requirement five is the constraint that makes this a genuine engineering problem: three peak enrollment weeks a year, the first week of each term, during which Course Registration cannot be down, cannot be mid-deployment, and cannot be the subject of any planned change at all. Every deployment window in this capstone has to be scheduled around those weeks, and a rollback plan has to exist and be rehearsed on paper before the very first production deployment — not invented after something breaks.

That's the requirements pass complete: instance strategy, Source Control, critical-path test coverage, Change Management integration, and the peak-enrollment timing constraint, all written down before a single test step exists. Next, Lesson 25 designs the actual ATF coverage for that critical path — a UI test simulating a student registering, a server-side test validating the capacity check, and a scheduled Test Suite tying it all together.
